transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-27 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Ellis, Priya Shah (Redwood); Maya Chen, Ravi Patel, Diego Alvarez (Lodestar)
--
Summary:
Quick product walkthrough focused on console telemetry for per-route usage, cost allocation and a proposed 'control room' view for finance and ml-ops. Discussed hosted vs dedicated pilot, compliance docs, and a short benchmarking window.
Topics:
- Per-route dashboards and tags
- Cost breakdown and chargeback patterns
- Usage analytics and anomaly detection
- Integration with Lodestar's billing/chargeback system
- Pilot options: hosted API pilot vs dedicated pool
- Security and compliance (SOC2, KMS, SSO)
- Next steps and benchmarks
--
Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um I'm Jordan with Redwood, this is Priya, our SE, and we're excited to show a quick tour of the console and the control-room view we put together for finance and ops.
[00:18] Maya (Lodestar): Thanks Jordan. We're mainly interested in where lineage of cost comes from, per-route, like chat vs embeddings, and how we can attach cost centers to product teams.
[00:28] Priya (Redwood): Totally, so at a high level we'll show the per-route dashboards, then the cost decomposition, and finally the control-room where you can pin alerts and run quick chargeback exports.
[00:40] Ravi (Lodestar): Quick clarification — our latency SLO is 120ms p50 at 2048 toks for the assistant route, and we want to see how batching and caching suggestions affect cost without breaking the SLO.
[00:54] Priya: Good — we'll highlight the suggestions tab in Optimize where the engine recommends batching thresholds, KV cache keys, and a quant profile; it estimates cost delta and latency impact.
[01:10] Diego: Also, can Redwood's console show chargeback by internal project tag? We use an internal tag set, e.g., team:recommendations, service:realtime.
[01:20] Priya: Yes, you can add custom route tags. In the demo we'll show tagging and how the chargeback export maps tags to billing lines.
[01:30] Speaker 1: (background) um yeah I can confirm that, that's in exports.
[01:35] Jordan: Alright Priya, take it away with the screen.
[02:05] Priya: Sharing screen now — okay, first screen is the Usage Overview, you can see total tokens by day, cost per day, and a top-line split between generation, embeddings, and rerank. Notice the traffic spike on the 14th — that was real example we seeded for demo.
[02:28] Priya: Switching to Routes, here's the per-route list. Each route shows p50/p95 latency, tokens per request, and cost per 1k requests. If you click a route you get a time-series and a table of sample requests for debugging.
[02:45] Maya: The sample requests are super helpful. Are those masked by default for PII?
[02:51] Priya: Yes, by default we mask user content in exports unless you enable a fuller debug mode; auditing is logged.
[03:04] Ravi: How do we map routes to our billing codes? We need to attach chargeback to projects and GL codes.
[03:10] Priya: In the Route Settings there's a 'Billing mapping' where you define mapping rules: tag -> GL code or cloud cost center. The export can then be pushed to your finance S3 bucket or to their API endpoint.
[03:22] Diego: What about multi-model fallbacks? We sometimes route to a cheaper quantized variant for non-critical queries.
[03:29] Priya: The console shows model variants per route and you can see fallback chains. The cost breakdown attributes tokens to the actual model used at inference time, and the routing policy column shows if a request fell back.
[03:45] Jordan: One note — when a fallback happens you can enable an alert so the team is notified; we also record the percent of fallbacks in the route trend.
[03:56] Maya: Great. Can you show the chargeback export for a single day with tag mapping?
[04:04] Priya: Sure. Going to Exports -> Chargeback -> create export. Selecting date 2026-03-14, include tags, group by project and route. Here's the CSV preview rows: timestamp, route, model, tokens_in, tokens_out, cost_usd, tag_project.
[04:25] Priya: (typing) download preview — okay, sending to chat — "preview csv link".
[04:30] Jordan: note: link is ephemeral, we'll attach permanent export to the pilot bucket.
[04:38] Ravi: On the Optimize side, can we see projected savings if we apply quantization and caching?
[04:44] Priya: Yes — under Optimize -> Recommendations we ran a small profile with your sample traffic. It shows estimated savings around 28% token-cost with a minimal 6% latency impact for the assistant route when enabling prefix-KV caching and int8 quant.
[05:00] Ravi: 6% latency is probably acceptable. How confident are those estimates?
[05:05] Priya: The estimates combine our runtime perf profiles (per model and hardware) plus your sampled latency distribution. For granular confidence we do a short benchmark on your traffic during the pilot.
[05:17] Maya: Security first — we need SOC2 Type II, SSO (SAML), encryption at rest with customer-managed keys, and exportable audit logs.
[05:28] Jordan: We have SOC2 docs, SAML is supported, and we integrate with AWS KMS or other HSMs for key control. We'll share the SOC2 summary and the KMS integration guide.
[05:40] Diego: For Private deployment: what's your path for on-prem or VPC? We're evaluating whether dedicated or private makes sense.
[05:48] Priya: Dedicated is reserved capacity in our managed cloud with isolated pools; Private is a customer-controlled VPC/private control plane option. For highly regulated workflows we recommend Private.
[05:59] Ravi: Timeline-wise, how long to spin a dedicated pool for pilot?
[06:03] Jordan: Usually 2-3 weeks for provisioning and configuration; for a quick hosted pilot it's near instant. For Private, it's longer — 6-8 weeks depending on network setup.
[06:14] Maya: Ok that's helpful. Can we see the anomaly detection for cost spikes? We had an incident where a bug caused runaway embedding calls.
[06:22] Priya: Navigate to Alerts -> Anomaly Detection. We show token spend z-score, burst detection and an incident timeline. You can set thresholds and auto-mitigations like temporary rate-limits or fallback to cheaper models.
[06:37] Diego: If we set auto-mitigation, does the system automatically change routes or just pause traffic?
[06:43] Priya: Currently you can set policy actions: throttle, route to cheaper variant, or block. Enterprise-only auto-rollbacks can also trigger a webhook to your orchestration system.
[06:55] Maya: Can we introspect request traces? We use tracing to debug latency regressions across services.
[07:02] Priya: We integrate with your tracing provider (Jaeger/Datadog). Each request in the console links to a trace id and shows the KV cache hit rate and server-side queue time.
[07:16] Speaker 2: (mumbled) that was super helpful.
[07:20] Priya: Next, I'll show the finance control-room mock. This is a pre-built dashboard that Lodestar's finance team could land on: high-level spend, top overrun routes, predicted monthly run-rate, and recommended mitigation actions.
[07:35] Priya: (scrolling) The panel allows you to hover into Top Routes by spend, see percent change week over week, and a waterfall that attributes cost to model type, quant level, and cached savings.
[07:50] Maya: That waterfall breakdown is exactly what we need for our monthly review meetings. Can we export a slide-ready summary?
[07:57] Priya: Yes, export to PDF or slide deck. There's a 'Finance Brief' template that compiles the waterfall, anomalies, and recommended action items.
[08:08] Ravi: About cost attribution accuracy — do you account for amortized reserved GPU costs when comparing hosted vs dedicated?
[08:16] Priya: Good question. For dedicated pools we allow you to input committed-cost numbers or attach your reserved instance amortization schedule. The console then shows true marginal cost and amortized unit cost.
[08:30] Diego: Any caveats on chargeback timing? We need daily granularity for internal billing.
[08:36] Jordan: Exports can be daily or hourly, and we support near-real-time streaming to your S3 or data warehouse.
[08:44] Maya: For the pilot, we'd like a 60-day window with daily exports and a benchmarking window.
[08:50] Jordan: Sounds good — we'll propose a pilot plan with two options.
[08:56] Priya: I'll also run a simulated workload in the sandbox to validate recommendations.
[09:02] Maya: Great. Slight side note — we use strict data retention policies, can Redwood redact logs after 30 days?
[09:09] Jordan: Retention rules are configurable per account and per route. We can purge or archive logs to your S3 with lifecycle rules.
[09:18] Ravi: One more technical — KV cache strategy: does Redwood persist KV cache across pods or is it local? We want cross-instance reuse.
[09:26] Priya: We have a distributed KV cache option for shared caches, which increases reuse at the cost of slightly higher network hop time; you'll see the tradeoff in the recommendation panel.
[09:40] Diego: Ok that helps.
[09:44] Priya: Moving on, here's the API panel — you can call the /v1/usage endpoint to pull per-route metrics programmatically. Also the SDKs have helpers to attach route tags at request time.
[09:59] Priya: Quick demo — making a call showing tags included in headers. (short pause) The logs show the request and cost attribution event appended.
[10:12] Maya: Perfect.
[10:15] Jordan: Alright, let's surface the actionable items in the control-room. You can create a runbook entry tied to a route. When a spike happens, the runbook shows steps: notify owner, reduce concurrency, enable fallback.
[10:29] Maya: We like that. Could that runbook be exported to our incident management system?
[10:33] Priya: Yes, runbooks can trigger PagerDuty or create a Jira ticket via integration.
[10:39] Ravi: On the benchmarking window — what telemetry do you pull during a benchmark?
[10:44] Priya: We collect request traces, microsecond-level latencies, kernel-level GPU metrics, token counts, and model utilization. We then produce a benchmark report comparing variants.
[10:58] Diego: Will you need credentials to our staging environment?
[11:02] Jordan: For the short benchmark, we typically ask for a small traffic replay or a sample of production traffic delivered to our secure ingestion endpoint. We'll sign an NDA and the data is masked and ephemeral.
[11:15] Maya: Okay, please include data handling details in the SOC2 package.
[11:19] Jordan: Will do.
[11:22] Speaker 1: (inaudible)
[11:25] Priya: Quick demo wrap-up — I created a placeholder pilot workspace for Lodestar in the sandbox, and I've pre-populated simulated routes: assistant/realtime, embedders/batch, and reranker/priority.
[11:40] Priya: (typing) I'm sending the sandbox access link now — look in the chat.
[11:46] Maya: Got it. Logging in... looks clean.
[11:50] Diego: Two last questions: 1) What SLAs do you guarantee for Hosted? 2) How do we request capacity increases during traffic surges?
[11:58] Jordan: Hosted has a 99.9% uptime SLA at the plan level and burst policies; Dedicated comes with higher SLAs depending on the commitment. Capacity increases can be configured with autoscaling policies and manual reserve requests — we also allow burst credits for short spikes.
[12:16] Maya: Good to know.
[12:18] Priya: Ok, before we end, quick recap and next steps.
[12:23] Jordan: Recap — Jordan will send pilot pricing and options; Priya will share recording, sandbox link, and the per-route demo snippet; Lodestar will share traffic profile and SLOs; schedule benchmark April 6-10.
[12:36] Ravi: Sounds good.
[12:39] Diego: We'll also loop in our security reviewer — I'll add them to the thread.
[12:43] Maya: Thanks everyone.
[12:45] Jordan: Thanks — we'll follow up with the pack.
[12:48] End meeting.

Notes on transcription: occasional crosstalk and a couple of inaudible segments. There were a few mis-attributed short interjections labeled as Speaker 1/2 in the transcript export. Shared artifacts: sandbox access link (ephemeral), preview CSV link, pilot plan draft (to be attached to email).
